warmup.q: The month-end report adds up every balance, which takes 30 seconds. While it runs, 5,000 payments each move money between two balances and finish. What does the report add up, and do the payments wait for it?
options: The payments wait until the report is done, and the report adds up the balances as they were when it started
A mix: each balance as it stood when the report happened to reach it, so the total is a little off
Every balance as it stood when the report started, and no payment waits
The payments fail with an error, because the report is reading their rows
warmup.why: Each payment writes a new copy of the balances it changes and leaves the old copies where they are. The report remembers which payments had finished when it started, and for every row it reads the copy that was current at that moment. So it needs no lock, and no payment waits. The second option is what you'd get with one copy of each row and no lock: a total that's off by every payment the report saw only half of. The first is how databases worked before they kept old copies. The last mixes this up with two payments that change the same row, which the third section covers.

sections.h: Counting while people pay: keep the old row
sections.html:
Let's put numbers on the scene. The app keeps its data in a database, a program that stores records and answers questions about them, asked in a language called SQL. The balances sit in a table called wallets, one row per customer, each with an id and a balance in cents. A card payment is a transfer: it takes money from one wallet and adds it to another. Each transfer runs as a transaction, a group of changes that the database applies all together or not at all.

The report reads 2 million rows in about 30 seconds, and about 9,000 transfers finish in that time. How can both run?

Version 1 makes them take turns. The report puts a lock on the table, a mark that says "wait until I'm done", and every transfer that wants to write waits. The total is right, and 9,000 transfers queue for up to 30 seconds. Card readers give up long before that.

Version 2 drops the lock, and the report reads whatever each row holds when it gets there. Halfway through, a transfer moves 250.00 from wallet 7 to wallet 1,800,000. The report read wallet 7 before the debit and reaches wallet 1,800,000 after the credit, so it counts that 250.00 twice. The next run is wrong by a different amount.

Version 3 never overwrites. Picture a notebook where nothing is ever rubbed out. To change a balance, you cross out the old line, write the new balance on a fresh line, and sign both. Someone who started reading at 18:00 can skip every change made after 18:00 and see the notebook as it stood then. A transfer in version 3 does the same. It writes a new version of the row, a complete copy with the new balance, and marks the old one "replaced by transaction 860". The report keeps a note of which transactions had finished when it started, called its snapshot, and for each row it reads the version that was current then. Nobody waits, and the total is exact.

This design is multi-version concurrency control (MVCC): keep several versions of each row, so that readers and writers can work at the same time. PostgreSQL, a free database program that many companies run, works this way. So do MySQL, another free database, and the database that the company Oracle sells. They keep the old versions in different places, as the last section shows.

Let's find the marks in PostgreSQL. Pages, tuples and heap files, in the Storage engines track, showed how PostgreSQL cuts a table's file, the heap, into 8 KB pages. Each page holds stored row versions, called tuples, in numbered slots. Every tuple starts with a header that holds two numbers. t_xmin is the id of the transaction that created this version. t_xmax is the id of the one that deleted or replaced it, or 0 while nobody has. A transaction id is a counter: each transaction that writes takes the next number.

So an UPDATE, the SQL command that changes rows, is a delete plus an insert. It writes its id into the old version's t_xmax and writes a complete new version with its id in t_xmin. It also points the old version's t_ctid field at the new one's address, so the versions of a row form a chain, oldest first. In the Try it, updating wallet 2 leaves slot 2 in place, stamped t_xmax = 858, and puts the new balance in slot 4.

The figure is the picture for this lesson: a chain of versions, each stamped with who created it and who ended it, and readers that each pick one. The notebook breaks at the picking. Its reader goes by the clock, and next we'll see why a database can't.

try.title: See both versions of an updated row
steps: From the labs folder, start PostgreSQL with docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait. (Docker runs programs in sealed boxes called containers, and this starts one with PostgreSQL inside.) Then open psql, PostgreSQL's command-line program where you type SQL: docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz.
Create a small wallets table with three rows, and read them with two hidden columns, xmin and xmax: the stamps from each tuple's header.

Update wallet 2. Predict: how many tuples does page 0 hold now, and what's in slot 2's t_xmax? Then read the page with heap_page_items, a function from the pageinspect extension that lists every tuple on a page, whether or not any reader can see it.

code.title: psql
code.html: CREATE TABLE wallets (id int PRIMARY KEY, balance_cents bigint) WITH (autovacuum_enabled = off); INSERT INTO wallets VALUES (1, 50000), (2, 50000), (3, 50000); SELECT ctid, xmin, xmax, * FROM wallets; UPDATE wallets SET balance_cents = balance_cents - 2500 WHERE id = 2; SELECT ctid, xmin, xmax, * FROM wallets; SELECT lp, t_xmin, t_xmax, t_ctid FROM heap_page_items(get_raw_page('wallets', 0));

try.expect:
ctid  | xmin | xmax | id | balance_cents
-------+------+------+----+---------------
 (0,1) |  857 |    0 |  1 |         50000
 (0,2) |  857 |    0 |  2 |         50000
 (0,3) |  857 |    0 |  3 |         50000

 ctid  | xmin | xmax | id | balance_cents
-------+------+------+----+---------------
 (0,1) |  857 |    0 |  1 |         50000
 (0,3) |  857 |    0 |  3 |         50000
 (0,4) |  858 |    0 |  2 |         47500

 lp | t_xmin | t_xmax | t_ctid
----+--------+--------+--------
  1 |    857 |      0 | (0,1)
  2 |    857 |    858 | (0,4)
  3 |    857 |      0 | (0,3)
  4 |    858 |      0 | (0,4)

xmin and xmax are system columns that every table has, and SELECT * leaves them out. ctid is a version's address: (page, slot). After the UPDATE, a query sees wallet 2 only at (0,4), written by transaction 858. The page still holds the old version in slot 2, stamped t_xmax = 858, with t_ctid pointing at slot 4: four tuples for three rows. Your ids will differ. The table was created with autovacuum_enabled = off, which stops the background cleanup of the fourth section from tidying the page before you look.

sections.h: Which version a reader sees: the snapshot and its rule
sections.html:
A reader needs a rule that picks exactly one version of every row. The notebook's rule was the clock: believe every line written before 18:00. A database would need the moment each transaction committed, and ids don't come in that order. (To commit is to end a transaction and make its changes count. To abort, or roll back, is to end it and throw them away.) In the Try it, transfer 859 starts first and commits last. A new customer's wallet, inserted by transaction 860, starts later and commits first. An id tells you who started first, not who finished first.

So PostgreSQL gives each reader a snapshot: a short note of which transactions count as finished for it. SELECT pg_current_snapshot() prints one in three parts, like 859:861:859:

  • The first number, the snapshot's xmin (859): every id below it had finished.
  • The second, its xmax (861): one past the newest id that had finished. Nothing from here up counts.
  • The list after the second colon: ids in between that were still running, here only 859.

A snapshot sees a transaction's changes if it committed, is below xmax and isn't on the running list. A transaction always sees its own changes. Add the two stamps on each tuple, and you get the visibility rule. A version is visible if the snapshot sees its creator (the id in t_xmin), and its deleter (in t_xmax) is 0 or not seen.

Let's apply it. Wallet 1's old version has xmin 857, xmax 859. For the snapshot 859:861:859, 857 committed long ago, so the creator is seen. 859 is on the running list, so the deleter isn't. The old version is visible, and the report reads 50,000. The new version, xmin 859, isn't visible, and it stays invisible after 859 commits, because 859 sits on this snapshot's list for good. Wallet 4, xmin 860, is visible, though 860 started after the transfer.

There's one question the snapshot can't answer: did that transaction commit or abort? PostgreSQL keeps the answer in the commit log, files called pg_xact with two bits per transaction id, for in progress, committed or aborted. COMMIT first makes its record in the write-ahead log safe on disk. (Write-ahead logging and crash recovery showed that log, where every change is written before the pages.) Then it sets its own two bits. It doesn't touch a single row, so committing one row costs the same as committing a million. An abort needs no undo either. Its bits say aborted, so its versions fail the rule for every snapshot.

When does a transaction take its snapshot? That's what its isolation level decides, a setting for how much of other transactions' work it may see. Under READ COMMITTED, PostgreSQL's default, every statement (every SQL command) takes a new snapshot, so it sees everything committed before it began. Under REPEATABLE READ, the first statement takes a snapshot and the transaction keeps it to the end. What a transaction promises: ACID and isolation levels showed what each level lets you see. Underneath, the only difference is when the snapshot is taken.

A transaction gets an id only when it first writes, so a read-only one never uses one up. Readers can now ignore writers. Next, we'll see what happens when two writers want the same row.

try.title: Watch a snapshot keep an old balance
steps: Open a second terminal in the labs folder and run the same psql command there. Keep both side by side: terminal 1 and terminal 2 below.

In terminal 1, start a transfer on wallet 1 and leave it open. In terminal 2, insert wallet 4, then start a REPEATABLE READ report, print its snapshot and read all the wallets. Predict the three parts of the snapshot, and whether the report sees wallet 4.
Commit in terminal 1. In terminal 2, read again and look at the page. Predict the report's answer for wallet 1. Then commit in terminal 2 and read once more.

code.title: two psql sessions
code.html: -- terminal 1: a slow transfer, left open BEGIN; UPDATE wallets SET balance_cents = balance_cents - 1000 WHERE id = 1; SELECT pg_current_xact_id() AS writer; -- terminal 2: a new customer's wallet, then a report INSERT INTO wallets VALUES (4, 50000); BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ; SELECT pg_current_snapshot(); SELECT id, balance_cents FROM wallets ORDER BY id; -- terminal 1 COMMIT; -- terminal 2 SELECT id, balance_cents FROM wallets ORDER BY id; SELECT lp, t_xmin, t_xmax, t_ctid FROM heap_page_items(get_raw_page('wallets', 0)); COMMIT; SELECT id, balance_cents FROM wallets ORDER BY id;

try.expect:
Terminal 1 prints writer = 859. Terminal 2 shows:

 pg_current_snapshot
---------------------
 859:861:859

 id | balance_cents
----+---------------
  1 |         50000
  2 |         47500
  3 |         50000
  4 |         50000

After terminal 1 commits, the report's query returns exactly the same four rows, while the page holds both versions of wallet 1:

 lp | t_xmin | t_xmax | t_ctid
----+--------+--------+--------
  1 |    857 |    859 | (0,5)
  2 |    857 |    858 | (0,4)
  3 |    857 |      0 | (0,3)
  4 |    858 |      0 | (0,4)
  5 |    859 |      0 | (0,5)
  6 |    860 |      0 | (0,6)

After its own COMMIT, terminal 2 reads wallet 1 as 49,000. The snapshot listed 859 as running, so the report kept slot 1 (its deleter, 859, is on the list) and skipped slot 5 (its creator, 859, is on the list), even after 859 committed. Wallet 4, in slot 6, was inserted by 860, which started after the transfer but committed before the snapshot was taken, so the report sees it. Your ids will differ.

sections.h: Two writers on one row: the second waits, then decides
sections.html:
Snapshots let readers ignore writers. Two writers can't ignore each other. Say transfer A takes 700 from wallet 3 while refund B adds 100 to it, at the same moment, and both read 50,000. If each wrote a new version on top of the one it read, wallet 3 would get two current versions, 49,300 and 50,100. One change would be lost. That bug is the lost update, from the lesson Lost updates: row locks, SKIP LOCKED and job queues.

So a writer must check the version it's about to replace, and PostgreSQL keeps that check in the version's t_xmax. When A updates wallet 3, it writes its id, 861, into the old version's t_xmax. That stamp is the row lock: "transaction 861 is replacing this version". When B reaches the same version, it finds a t_xmax that belongs to a transaction still in progress. It doesn't write over it. It waits for A to end.

PostgreSQL keeps no list of locked rows in memory, which could run out with millions of rows locked. The lock is in the row itself, and B waits on A's transaction id. The next lesson, Concurrency control, watches that wait from the inside.

When A ends, B's next move depends on how A ended and on B's isolation level:

  • If A aborted, its t_xmax means nothing. B updates the version it found.
  • If A committed and B runs READ COMMITTED, B follows t_ctid to A's new version. It checks its WHERE clause (the condition that picks the rows) again on that version, and applies its change there. 49,300 + 100 = 49,400, and nothing is lost.
  • If A committed and B runs REPEATABLE READ, B can't do that. Its snapshot says A's version doesn't exist, and changing a version you can't see would break the snapshot. PostgreSQL aborts B with could not serialize access due to concurrent update. Its SQLSTATE, the standard five-character error code, is 40001, which tells the program to run the whole transaction again.

This rule is called first-updater-wins. The first transaction to stamp t_xmax gets the row, and the second waits to learn whether it may go on. The lab's store can't wait yet. It fails the second writer at once with WriteConflict, whenever a transaction it can't see has touched the row and hasn't aborted.

So the slogan of MVCC, "readers don't block writers, and writers don't block readers", is true, and it's only half the story. Snapshots free the readers. Writers of one row still take turns. And every version a writer replaces stays behind on the page. Next, we'll see who throws them away.

try.title: Make a second writer wait, then fail
steps: Terminal 1: start transfer A on wallet 3 and leave it open.
Terminal 2: start a REPEATABLE READ transaction, read wallet 3, look at slot 3's stamps, then update wallet 3. Predict: does the UPDATE come back?
Commit in terminal 1 and watch terminal 2. Roll terminal 2 back. Then run the same race with READ COMMITTED in terminal 2, and predict the balance it returns.

code.title: two psql sessions
code.html: -- terminal 1: transfer A, left open BEGIN; UPDATE wallets SET balance_cents = balance_cents - 700 WHERE id = 3; -- terminal 2: refund B under REPEATABLE READ BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ; SELECT balance_cents FROM wallets WHERE id = 3; SELECT lp, t_xmin, t_xmax FROM heap_page_items(get_raw_page('wallets', 0)) WHERE lp = 3; UPDATE wallets SET balance_cents = balance_cents + 100 WHERE id = 3; -- waits -- terminal 1 COMMIT; -- terminal 2: the UPDATE has failed; end the transaction ROLLBACK; -- the same race with READ COMMITTED, the default, in terminal 2 -- terminal 1 BEGIN; UPDATE wallets SET balance_cents = balance_cents - 700 WHERE id = 3; -- terminal 2 BEGIN; UPDATE wallets SET balance_cents = balance_cents + 100 WHERE id = 3 RETURNING balance_cents; -- waits -- terminal 1 COMMIT; -- terminal 2 COMMIT;

try.expect:
The refund reads 50,000, and slot 3 already carries A's id in t_xmax, though A hasn't committed:

 lp | t_xmin | t_xmax
----+--------+--------
  3 |    857 |    861

The REPEATABLE READ UPDATE hangs. The moment terminal 1 commits, it fails:

ERROR:  could not serialize access due to concurrent update

In the READ COMMITTED round, the UPDATE also hangs, then succeeds when terminal 1 commits, on top of A's new version:

 balance_cents
---------------
         48700

50,000 minus two transfers of 700 is 48,600, plus the refund's 100 is 48,700: nothing was lost. Your ids will differ.

sections.h: Throwing old versions away: VACUUM, the horizon and freezing
sections.html:
Every UPDATE leaves its old version behind. In the Try it, a table of 10,000 rows updated twice holds 20,000 dead versions, and its file grows from 55 pages to 163. Something must clean up, and it must know when a version is safe to remove. In PostgreSQL, that's VACUUM, a command that removes dead versions, and autovacuum, a helper that runs VACUUM in the background once a table has changed enough.

A version is safe to remove when no snapshot can ever see it again. Its deleter must have committed, and every snapshot still in use must have been taken after that. PostgreSQL tracks this with one number, the horizon: the lowest xmin of any snapshot in use, or of any transaction still running. Every id below the horizon had finished before any of those snapshots was taken. So a version whose deleter committed below the horizon is invisible to every snapshot, now and later, and VACUUM may remove it. A version created by an aborted transaction can go at once.

One number for the whole database makes a long transaction costly. In the Try it, one REPEATABLE READ report stays open while the updates run, and VACUUM reports 20000 are dead but not yet removable. The report can't see those versions either: they were created and deleted after its snapshot. But VACUUM only compares with the horizon, so it keeps them all. When the report commits, the same VACUUM removes all 20,000.

The usual culprits are a REPEATABLE READ transaction left open, and a transaction that wrote something and then sat idle in transaction. That means it's still open and running nothing, while the program behind it does something else. A READ COMMITTED transaction that has only read holds the horizon back only while a statement runs.

Removing a dead version works the way Pages, tuples and heap files showed for a delete. First VACUUM removes the entries that point at it from the table's indexes, the lookup structures that find a row by its key. Then it marks the slot unused, packs the page's rows together and notes the free space. It doesn't shrink the file. The table is still 163 pages afterwards, and the free space holds the next updates.

A HOT update (heap-only tuple) is a shortcut. If no indexed column changed and the new version fit on the same page, no new index entry was written. VACUUM then leaves the old slot as a pointer to the new one, so the index still finds the row.

VACUUM's second job is about the ids. They're 32-bit numbers, compared in a circle: for any id, the 2 billion before it count as the past, and the 2 billion after it as the future. A busy database that commits 2,000 writing transactions a second uses 2 billion ids in under 12 days. Then a version written 2 billion transactions ago would look as if it came from the future, and vanish. So VACUUM freezes old versions: it marks them "committed, visible to every snapshot", and nobody reads their t_xmin again.

Autovacuum forces a freezing pass on any table whose oldest unfrozen id is more than 200 million transactions old (the setting autovacuum_freeze_max_age). If freezing falls behind, PostgreSQL starts warning 40 million ids before the limit. With 3 million left, it refuses to start any transaction that would need a new id. The stepper follows one row from UPDATE to freezing.

Next, we'll see where MySQL and Oracle keep their old versions instead.

frames.say: Months later, the counter has moved on by hundreds of millions. Autovacuum notices that the table's oldest unfrozen id, its relfrozenxid, is older than autovacuum_freeze_max_age. Ids are 32-bit and compared in a circle, so in about 2 billion more transactions 860 would look like an id from the future, and slot 2 would vanish. Before that, VACUUM freezes slot 2: it sets a flag that says "committed, visible to everyone". From then on, nobody looks at its xmin again.

try.title: Hold VACUUM back with one open report
steps: Terminal 1: open a REPEATABLE READ report and run one query, which takes its snapshot. Leave it open.

Terminal 2: create settlements, a table of 10,000 small amounts, and update every row twice. Check the table's size and its count of dead versions, then run VACUUM (VERBOSE), which prints what it did. Predict how many dead versions it removes.
Commit terminal 1 and vacuum again. Then compare the table's age(relfrozenxid), how many transactions old its oldest unfrozen id is, before and after VACUUM (FREEZE).

code.title: two psql sessions
code.html: -- terminal 1: a report that stays open BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ; SELECT sum(balance_cents) FROM wallets; -- terminal 2: make 20,000 dead versions, then vacuum CREATE TABLE settlements (id int PRIMARY KEY, amount_cents bigint) WITH (autovacuum_enabled = off); INSERT INTO settlements SELECT g, 1000 FROM generate_series(1, 10000) g; SELECT pg_relation_size('settlements') / 8192 AS pages; UPDATE settlements SET amount_cents = amount_cents + 1; UPDATE settlements SET amount_cents = amount_cents + 1; SELECT pg_relation_size('settlements') / 8192 AS pages; SELECT pg_stat_force_next_flush(); SELECT n_live_tup, n_dead_tup FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname = 'settlements'; VACUUM (VERBOSE) settlements; -- terminal 1 COMMIT; -- terminal 2: vacuum again, then freeze VACUUM (VERBOSE) settlements; SELECT pg_relation_size('settlements') / 8192 AS pages; SELECT count(DISTINCT (ctid::text::point)[0]) AS pages_with_rows FROM settlements; SELECT age(relfrozenxid) FROM pg_class WHERE relname = 'settlements'; VACUUM (FREEZE) settlements; SELECT age(relfrozenxid) FROM pg_class WHERE relname = 'settlements'; SELECT t_xmin, combined_flags FROM heap_page_items(get_raw_page('settlements', 162)), LATERAL heap_tuple_infomask_flags(t_infomask, t_infomask2) WHERE lp_flags = 1 LIMIT 1; SHOW autovacuum_freeze_max_age;

try.expect:
The table grows from 55 pages to 163, and the statistics count the dead versions (pg_stat_force_next_flush() brings the counters up to date at once):

 n_live_tup | n_dead_tup
------------+------------
      10000 |      20000

The first VACUUM, with the report open, removes nothing:

tuples: 0 removed, 30000 remain, 20000 are dead but not yet removable
removable cutoff: 873, which was 4 XIDs old when operation ended

After the report commits:

tuples: 20000 removed, 10000 remain, 0 are dead but not yet removable
removable cutoff: 879, which was 4 XIDs old when operation ended
visibility map: 163 pages set all-visible, 108 pages set all-frozen (0 were all-visible)

(output trimmed). removable cutoff is the horizon. The file is still 163 pages, but only 55 of them hold rows. The other 108 are empty and ready for the next updates, which is also why VACUUM could mark 108 pages all-frozen. Then the freeze: age(relfrozenxid) goes from 8 to 0, and a live tuple keeps its t_xmin but is flagged frozen:

 t_xmin |   combined_flags
--------+--------------------
    876 | {HEAP_XMIN_FROZEN}

 autovacuum_freeze_max_age
---------------------------
 200000000

Your ids will differ. When you're done with this lesson, drop the two tables (DROP TABLE wallets, settlements;) or delete the whole database with docker compose -f env/postgres.yml down -v.

aside.title: Why doesn't COMMIT throw the old version away?
aside.html: It would be tidy, and it would be wrong. When a transaction commits, other readers may still hold snapshots from before it, and they need the version it replaced. COMMIT can't tell who they are without asking every open transaction, which would slow down every commit. So COMMIT only flips two bits, and the cleanup waits for VACUUM, which compares one number, the horizon, for a whole table at once. Doing the work later and in bulk keeps each commit fast.

sections.h: Where the old versions live: in the table, or in an undo log
sections.html:
Every MVCC database keeps old versions for old snapshots. Where it keeps them decides who pays for them, and what a long-open transaction breaks.

PostgreSQL keeps every version in the table itself, oldest first, each a complete copy of the row. An old snapshot reads its version directly, and everyone else pays. Scans step over dead versions, an update that isn't HOT adds entries to every index, and VACUUM must visit the table and its indexes to clean up.

MySQL stores its rows through InnoDB, the part of MySQL that keeps tables on disk, and InnoDB does the opposite. It changes the row in place, in the tree of pages that holds the table's rows in key order. (InnoDB calls it the clustered index.) Before it overwrites the row, it copies the old values of the changed columns into an undo log, a separate store of what each row was before. Each row carries two hidden fields for this. DB_TRX_ID names the last transaction that wrote it, and DB_ROLL_PTR points at the undo record that holds the values from before that write. A reader whose snapshot is older than the row follows those pointers back and rebuilds the version it should see.

The table stays compact, and the old reader pays: the older its snapshot, the longer the chain it walks. A background job called purge throws away undo records once no snapshot can need them. It's InnoDB's VACUUM.

Oracle works like InnoDB. It changes rows in place, keeps the old images in undo, and rebuilds the data as it was when the query started. It keeps undo for a set time and then reuses the space. A long query that needs undo that's already been reused fails with the error ORA-01555, "snapshot too old".

So one long-open transaction hurts each database in a different place:

PostgreSQL MySQL (InnoDB) Oracle
old versions live in the table and its indexes the undo log undo
a long transaction holds back VACUUM in every table holds back purge may lose the undo it needs
the symptom bloat: tables and indexes grow the history list and the undo log grow ORA-01555 for the long query

Bloat is space in a table's file taken up by dead versions. In PostgreSQL, the damage outlives the transaction. Once a table has grown, VACUUM makes the space reusable inside the file but doesn't give it back. A table bloated by a session left idle in transaction all weekend stays large until it's rewritten.

In InnoDB, the Try it holds one snapshot open while a thousand small updates commit. The history list length, InnoDB's count of committed transactions whose undo purge hasn't thrown away yet, climbs to about a thousand. It stays there until the snapshot closes. The MySQL docs warn that this happens even when the long transaction only reads. An old snapshot is never free. Close each transaction as soon as its work is done.

That's the limit of MVCC, too. It frees the readers, but every old version costs space until the oldest snapshot lets go, and writers of one row still wait. The next lesson opens that waiting.

try.title: Hold back InnoDB's purge with one open snapshot
steps: From the labs folder, start MySQL 8.4: docker compose -f env/mysql.yml up -d --wait. Its settlements table has 10,000 rows of 1,000 cents each. Open two terminals there.
Terminal 1: run docker compose -f env/mysql.yml exec db mysql course, which opens MySQL's command-line program. Start a transaction with a consistent snapshot and read the total. Leave it open.

Terminal 2: run 1,000 single-row updates, each its own transaction, then read InnoDB's history list length and the total. Predict both, and what terminal 1's next read returns. Then commit terminal 1 and check the history list again for half a minute. Stop MySQL afterwards: docker compose -f env/mysql.yml down -v.

code.title: two terminals in the labs folder
code.html: # terminal 1, inside mysql START TRANSACTION WITH CONSISTENT SNAPSHOT; SELECT sum(amount_cents) AS total FROM settlements; # terminal 2: 1,000 transactions, one UPDATE each for i in $(seq 1 1000); do echo "UPDATE settlements SET amount_cents = amount_cents + 1 WHERE id = $i;" done | docker compose -f env/mysql.yml exec -T db mysql course docker compose -f env/mysql.yml exec db mysql course -e " SELECT name, count FROM information_schema.INNODB_METRICS WHERE name = 'trx_rseg_history_len'; SELECT sum(amount_cents) AS total FROM settlements;" # terminal 1 SELECT sum(amount_cents) AS total FROM settlements; COMMIT; # terminal 2, a few times over the next 30 seconds docker compose -f env/mysql.yml exec db mysql course -e " SELECT name, count FROM information_schema.INNODB_METRICS WHERE name = 'trx_rseg_history_len';"

try.expect:
Terminal 1's first read shows 10000000. After the updates, terminal 2 sees (output trimmed):

+----------------------+-------+
| name                 | count |
+----------------------+-------+
| trx_rseg_history_len |  1001 |
+----------------------+-------+
+----------+
| total    |
+----------+
| 10001000 |
+----------+

Terminal 1 still reads 10000000: InnoDB rebuilds the old versions from undo records that purge isn't allowed to throw away. After terminal 1 commits, the count stays at 1001 for a few seconds and then drops to 0 as purge catches up (within about 20 seconds here). Run the 1,000 updates again with no snapshot open, and the count stays in single digits throughout: purge keeps up as long as nothing holds it back.

mistake: A common mistake is to treat VACUUM as a chore about disk space that can be switched off or put off. A team turns autovacuum off on its busiest table because it uses the disk at peak hours, or a session sits idle in transaction for a day. Dead versions pile up. Every scan reads through them, every update that isn't HOT adds index entries, and queries slow down while the data stays the same. Left long enough, the oldest unfrozen id nears the limit, autovacuum forces a big freezing pass at the worst moment, and in the end the server stops handing out transaction ids. Leave autovacuum on, and tune it per table instead. For a big, busy table, lower autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor from its default of 20% of the table, so cleanup starts sooner. And watch for long transactions and for age(datfrozenxid), the age of the oldest unfrozen id in the database.
opening:
Picture the coffee-shop payments app at the end of the month. A report adds up all 2 million customers' balances, which takes 30 seconds. Meanwhile, 300 times a second, a payment moves money from one balance to another. No payment creates or destroys money, so the total must be exact.

It is, and not one payment waited for the report. Yet it read rows that were changing under it.

It's natural to picture a table as one copy of each row, which an update overwrites like a variable. With one copy, you'd have to choose: make the payments wait, or add up a mix of old and new.

In Write skew and phantoms, each booking ran as a transaction (a group of changes that counts as one) and read the table as it stood at one moment. We never asked how. In this lesson, we'll watch an update leave the old row behind, work out which copy each reader picks, and follow the cleanup that one forgotten transaction stalls. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a month-end report that added up 2 million balances while payments kept moving money, and nobody waited. Every payment left the old version of its rows behind, and the report's snapshot told it which version to read. The bill comes later, as cleanup that one open transaction can hold back for the whole database.

On any PostgreSQL database you can reach, run SELECT pid, state, xact_start FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE xact_start IS NOT NULL ORDER BY xact_start;. The first row is the oldest open transaction. Ask what it's waiting for.

Next, we'll open the locks that make writers take turns, and find out what happens when two transactions each wait for the other.

compare.title: Where the old version lives: PostgreSQL vs InnoDB

a.label: PostgreSQL
a.title: versions in the table
a.html:
UPDATE wallet 7 SET balance = 250.00

heap page:
  slot 1  500.00  xmin 850  xmax 860  -> slot 2
  slot 2  250.00  xmin 860  xmax 0

old version: a whole copy of the row,
  in the table, oldest first
old snapshot: reads slot 1 directly
new index entry: only if not HOT
cleanup: VACUUM, of table and indexes

b.label: MySQL InnoDB
b.title: newest in place, old values in undo
b.html:
UPDATE wallet 7 SET balance = 250.00

clustered index leaf:
  wallet 7  250.00  DB_TRX_ID 860
            DB_ROLL_PTR -> undo record
undo log:
  wallet 7  balance was 500.00

old version: only the changed columns,
  in the undo log, newest first
old snapshot: rebuilds 500.00 from undo
new index entry: only if a key changed
cleanup: purge, of the undo log

compare.note: Both keep old versions for old snapshots, and they differ in who pays. PostgreSQL copies the whole row on every update and leaves the old copy in the table, so scans step over dead versions until VACUUM runs, and an update that isn't HOT writes to every index. InnoDB changes the row in place and writes a small undo record, so the table stays compact. A reader with an old snapshot pays instead, walking undo records back from the newest version, and a long transaction makes the undo log grow and holds back purge. Oracle follows the InnoDB design.

worked.title: Work out what three snapshots see

steps.say: Wallet 7 has three versions. The commit log says 850 and 860 committed and 875 aborted. Three readers took their snapshots at different times. For each one, we ask the visibility rule's two questions: is the creator seen, and is the deleter seen?
steps.code:
slot 1  500.00  xmin 850  xmax 860
slot 2  250.00  xmin 860  xmax 875
slot 3  100.00  xmin 875  xmax 0

S1 = 860:861:860     taken while 860 ran
S2 = 875:876:875     taken while 875 ran
S3 = 880:880:        taken after 875 aborted

steps.say: S1. Slot 1: 850 is below S1's xmin of 860 and committed, so the creator is seen. Its deleter, 860, is on the running list, so it isn't. Slot 1 is visible, and S1 reads 500.00. Slots 2 and 3 were created by 860 and 875, which S1 can't see.
steps.code: fun sees(s: Snapshot, xid: Long) = xid == s.owner || (xid < s.xmax && xid !in s.active && status(xid) == COMMITTED) sees(S1, 850) == true // slot 1's creator sees(S1, 860) == false // slot 1's deleter: on S1's running list

steps.say: S2. Slot 1's deleter, 860, is below 875 and committed, so slot 1 is deleted for S2. Slot 2's creator, 860, is seen, and its deleter, 875, is on the running list. S2 reads 250.00, and it would go on reading 250.00 after 875 finished.
steps.code: isVisible(slot1, S2) == false // 860 deleted it, and S2 sees 860 isVisible(slot2, S2) == true // 875 is running for S2

steps.say: S3. 875 aborted, so S3 doesn't see it, as creator or as deleter. Slot 3 is invisible, and slot 2 is visible again: a deleter that aborted counts as no deleter. S3 reads 250.00. No undo ran; the commit log alone did it.
steps.code: isVisible(slot2, S3) == true // xmax 875 aborted: ignored isVisible(slot3, S3) == false // xmin 875 aborted

steps.say: Now VACUUM runs while S1 is still open. The horizon is S1's xmin, 860. Slot 1's deleter, 860, isn't below 860, so slot 1 stays, and slot 2 is live. Slot 3 can go at once: its creator aborted, so no snapshot will ever see it.
steps.code:
horizon = 860
slot 1: xmax 860 committed, but 860 >= 860   -> keep
slot 2: xmax 875 aborted                     -> live, keep
slot 3: xmin 875 aborted                     -> remove

lab.title: Build a multi-version store with snapshots and VACUUM
steps: Read the class comment of MvccStore.kt and everything below its "provided" line. begin takes the snapshot, commit and abort only write the commit log, and horizon returns the oldest snapshot's xmin.
Run the tests once. All 13 fail.
Write sees and isVisible, the visibility rule, then get. The tests about snapshots, your own writes and aborted transactions pass.

Write checkWritable, put and delete. The conflict tests pass, and so does the write-skew test. Read that one: it passes only because your store allows the anomaly. The next lesson shows how SERIALIZABLE catches it.
Write vacuum, and run the tests until all 13 pass.
hints: In sees, check xid >= snapshot.xmax and xid in snapshot.active before you ask the commit log. A transaction that committed after the snapshot was taken says COMMITTED in the log, and it must still be invisible.
In get, put and delete, get the snapshot with statementSnapshot(tx), never tx.snapshot directly. That one call is the whole difference between READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ.

checkWritable needs one test for both cases of the third section, Two writers on one row. A writer you can't see is either still running (PostgreSQL would wait) or committed after your snapshot (REPEATABLE READ fails). Skip ids that aborted.

In vacuum, compare xmax < horizon(), strictly. A version whose xmax equals the horizon was deleted by a transaction that was running when the oldest snapshot was taken, so that snapshot may still need it.

drill.title: Write the visibility rule from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write sees(snapshot, xid) and isVisible(version, snapshot) for a snapshot of (owner, xmin, xmax, active) and a version of (xmin, xmax), given status(xid) from the commit log. Then say which check makes REPEATABLE READ repeatable.

answer.html: fun sees(s: Snapshot, xid: Long): Boolean { if (xid == s.owner) return true // my own changes if (xid >= s.xmax) return false // not finished when I took the snapshot if (xid in s.active) return false // running when I took it return status(xid) == TxStatus.COMMITTED // finished: visible only if it committed } fun isVisible(v: Version, s: Snapshot): Boolean = sees(s, v.xmin) && !(v.xmax != 0L && sees(s, v.xmax)) // The `xid in s.active` and `xid >= s.xmax` checks: a transaction that was running when the // snapshot was taken stays invisible after it commits, so reading again gives the same answer.

recap: In PostgreSQL, an UPDATE writes a whole new version of the row and stamps the old one's t_xmax with its transaction id. The old version stays, so readers don't wait for writers and writers don't wait for readers.
A snapshot is xmin:xmax:running list. A version is visible if the snapshot sees its creator and its deleter is 0 or not seen. COMMIT only sets two bits in the commit log.
READ COMMITTED takes a new snapshot for every statement. REPEATABLE READ takes one for the whole transaction.
Writers of one row still take turns: the row lock is the old version's t_xmax. A second writer waits, and under REPEATABLE READ it fails with 40001 if the first one committed.

VACUUM removes versions whose deleter committed below the horizon, the oldest snapshot in use, so one long transaction holds back cleanup in every table, and the file doesn't shrink. VACUUM also freezes old versions before the 32-bit ids wrap around, and autovacuum forces that at 200 million ids of age.

The limit: MVCC frees readers only. Writers of the same row still wait, write skew still slips through, and every old version costs space somewhere (the table in PostgreSQL, undo in MySQL and Oracle) until the oldest snapshot lets go.

explain.prompt: A friend says: "PostgreSQL keeps old versions of rows, so it never locks rows. That's why two refunds of the same payment can't block each other." Explain what really happens.
explain.answer: Keeping old versions means readers need no locks: a reader picks the version of each row that its snapshot can see, and writers never wait for readers. Writers still lock. An UPDATE stamps the old version's t_xmax with its transaction id, and that stamp is the row lock. A second refund that reaches the same version finds a t_xmax that belongs to a transaction still running, and waits for it to end. If the first refund commits, the second one, under READ COMMITTED, reads the new version and applies its change on top. Under REPEATABLE READ it fails with a serialization error and must be run again. So two refunds of one payment do block each other, one after the other, and that's what stops one of them from being lost.

deeper.html:
Hint bits. Asking the commit log about every tuple would be slow. So the first reader that learns a tuple's creator or deleter committed (or aborted) writes that answer into the tuple header as a hint bit, and later readers skip the lookup. This is why a plain SELECT can write to a page: it's setting hint bits, not changing data.

VACUUM's other two jobs. PostgreSQL's routine-vacuuming docs give four reasons to vacuum. Two are in this lesson: removing dead versions and preventing wraparound. The third is the visibility map, two bits per heap page saying "every tuple here is visible to everyone" and "every tuple here is frozen". An index-only scan answers a query from the index alone, but it may skip reading a heap page only if that page's all-visible bit is set, and only VACUUM sets it. So a table that's rarely vacuumed gets slow index-only scans. The fourth is statistics: VACUUM ANALYZE and autovacuum's analyze step refresh the numbers the planner uses to choose how to run a query.

One more holder of the horizon. A replica, a copy of the database kept up to date on another machine, can run queries too. With hot_standby_feedback on, it tells the main server about its oldest query, so a long report on the replica holds back VACUUM on the main server.

The cost of keeping whole copies. Andy Pavlo and Bohan Zhang's post on PostgreSQL's MVCC gives an example of 10 million live tuples and 40 million dead ones: a 50 GB table holding 10 GB of live data. Their complaints are the same trade-offs as the compare block: full-row copies, version chains ordered oldest to newest, every index touched by an update that isn't HOT, and autovacuum that is hard to tune. Leaving free space on each page with fillfactor (the Try it of Pages, tuples and heap files set it to 80) makes HOT updates more likely.

Multixacts. One t_xmax holds one id, but several transactions can lock the same row in share mode at once (SELECT ... FOR SHARE, or the checks behind a foreign key). PostgreSQL then stores a multixact id in t_xmax, which points to a list of lockers. Multixact ids are 32-bit too and need their own freezing, which is why the docs also speak of multixact ID wraparound.

Finding the transaction that holds things back. In PostgreSQL, SELECT pid, state, xact_start, backend_xmin FROM pg_stat_activity ORDER BY age(backend_xmin) DESC NULLS LAST lists sessions by how old a snapshot they hold. Two holders don't show up there: a replication slot's xmin in pg_replication_slots, and a prepared transaction in pg_prepared_xacts, which survives restarts and keeps its snapshot until someone commits or rolls it back (Atomic commit across machines, lesson 7 of this track, makes one on purpose). In MySQL, SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS prints the history list length and the oldest open transactions.
